tables.how: Every Board file whose target is a money file (a contract, lease, grant agreement, loan, settlement with a business, accepted grant, emergency contract or appropriation; 3,907 files introduced since 2014) that has a recorded final Board roll call, read through the shared roll-call reader (scripts/lib/rollcalls.py): the last Board roll call on the measure itself, with a file whose final passage is printed without names left out. 3,483 files: 3,359 passed with no one voting no (2,703 with every listed member voting aye), 121 passed over at least one no and 3 were voted down; the amounts add up to $66,594,357,526. The column of files on the same vote list reproduces the case’s groups: 2,983 final votes sit in 312 same-day lists of five or more, the largest 44 files on 2015-12-08. The department and the organization are read by machine from the title; where the title names neither (most appropriation ordinances, and settlements with private persons), the department column says the City. Private persons and family trusts are never named.
tables.limits: A unanimous vote is the ordinary result and no sign of anything wrong; a no vote is ordinary too, and the vote pages give no reasons. Amounts are the totals the titles name: an amended agreement counts again at each new total, rent and accepted grants are money coming to the City, and budget ordinances name no single figure. Two files with the same date and the same line-up may have been one consent-agenda roll call or two separate votes; the record cannot tell them apart. “Excused” is printed both for a member out of the room and for one excused from voting. 423 more money files have no recorded Board vote and are not listed here; 17 roll calls remain without member votes in any record (see the list of roll calls whose vote page names nobody).

A party is in the donor circle when the organization, or donors naming it as employer, gave to the member’s committees before the vote. A private party is counted and not named.
tables.limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. Donors give to members who already agree with them, so voting a donor’s way is expected without any exchange. The pairs from one roll call are not independent; the analysis compares each member with the other members on the same roll call and finds nothing beyond chance.

tables.how: The lobbyist analysis’s widest vote test, as the case quotes it: 307 final votes and 3,297 member votes. Members voted the client’s way in 95.5% of 426 votes where the client’s circle had given to them in the two years before and in 91.5% of 2,871 where it had not. The same rows are in the evidence for the case on lobby money.
tables.limits: Nearly every vote here is an aye on a matter that passed without dissent, so a member who received money and one who did not vote alike; only the divided roll calls can show a difference, and they are few. A lobbyist contacts the members most likely to matter and donors give to members who already agree with them, so even a gap would not show that money moved a vote. The client’s side is read from a few typed words, or from the title of a money file matched to a client by name, and a measure can be amended between the contact and the vote. Members printed as excused or absent are left out: the page does not say whether they stepped aside or were out of the room. The money column adds contributions from the client, its officers, its lobbyists, their firm and the firm’s staff; the individual contributions are in the list of contributions above. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made.
